Multinomial LASSO lambda.1se from cross-validation 0.495 0.505 Sparse and interpretable, but accuracy is lower and it tends to over-shrink coefficients.
Multinomial Logistic Regression after LASSO Words selected by multinomial LASSO 0.590 0.410 More flexible after screening and still interpretable, but less stable and more prone to confusion across nearby classes.
Multiclass Neural Network Best architecture from 3.3(b): NN3, epoch = 15 0.400 0.600 Best predictive performance here and captures nonlinear patterns, but is the least interpretable.

(b) Recommendation

Which bag-of-words model would you recommend for the five-class problem? Explain your choice. I would recommend the multiclass neural network for the five-class bag-of-words problem. Among the three models, it achieves the highest testing accuracy (0.615) and the lowest testing error (0.385), so it performs best as a predictor on unseen data. The multinomial LASSO is more interpretable, but its accuracy is noticeably lower, and the multinomial logistic regression after LASSO performs worst of the three. Since the goal here is prediction across five rating categories, the neural network offers the best balance in terms of predictive performance, even though it is less interpretable than the regression-based alternatives.

Part 4: Transformer-Based Models with LLMs

Instead of using the Bag of Words (BoW) approach, we now apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict the five rating categories, leveraging their ability to capture deep contextual and semantic information from the text—far beyond what traditional models like BoW can achieve.

To do this, we use Hugging Face, a widely adopted platform that provides easy access to pretrained transformer models and tools for fine-tuning them on custom datasets. Hugging Face simplifies the process of loading models, tokenizing text, and integrating advanced architectures into machine learning workflows.

At the core of most LLMs is the transformer, a deep learning architecture that uses self-attention mechanisms to model relationships between words across a sentence. In this section, we focus on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), a popular transformer model that reads text bidirectionally—meaning it learns context from both the left and the right of each word simultaneously—enabling a much deeper understanding of language.

Rather than using BERT as an end-to-end classifier, we will extract its sentence embeddings—dense vector representations of the text—and use them as features for downstream models such as LASSO or other classification algorithms. This approach allows us to combine the expressive power of LLMs with the interpretability and flexibility of classical models.

4.1 Sentiment pipeline

Use the transformers package to get predicted 5-star ratings for the reviews in the testing data.

(a) Build the pipeline

Apply the text-classification task with model nlptown/bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment. Remember to set truncation = TRUE and max_length = as.integer(512).

star_predictor <- transformers$pipeline(
  "text-classification",
  model = 'nlptown/bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment',
  truncation = TRUE,
  max_length = as.integer(512)
)

(b) Generate predictions

Extract the predicted star label for each review in the testing data.

test_texts <- as.list(yelp_data_1200$text[test_idx])
predictions <- star_predictor(test_texts)

(c) Evaluate the pipeline

Report:

  • testing accuracy,
  • testing mis-classification error,
  • and the confusion matrix.
# Extract number from prediction labels
pred_labels <- sapply(predictions, function(x) as.integer(substr(x$label, 1, 1)))
true_labels <- yelp_data_1200$stars[test_idx]

# Compute metrics
acc <- mean(pred_labels == true_labels)
err <- 1 - acc
cat("Testing accuracy:", acc, "\n")
## Testing accuracy: 0.62
cat("Testing misclassification error:", err, "\n")
## Testing misclassification error: 0.38
table(Predicted = pred_labels, Actual = true_labels)
##          Actual
## Predicted  1  2  3  4  5
##         1 21  1  0  2  1
##         2  6  4  5  2  1
##         3  0  2 10  4  2
##         4  1  2 12 22 17
##         5  0  0  2 16 67

(d) Short discussion

In 5 sentences, describe what this pipeline is doing well and where it appears to struggle.

The sentiment pipeline achieves a testing accuracy of 0.62, which is reasonable given that it is a pretrained model applied directly to Yelp reviews without any task-specific fine-tuning. The model performs best at the extremes, correctly classifying 21 out of 28 one-star reviews and 67 out of 85 five-star reviews, suggesting it reliably captures clearly negative and clearly positive sentiment. The main struggle is in the middle ratings of 2, 3, and 4 stars, where reviews mix positive and negative language in varying degrees that are difficult to distinguish. The most common errors are off by just one star, such as predicting 4 when the true label is 3 or predicting 3 when the true label is 4, indicating the model understands general sentiment direction but lacks precision on intensity. Errors of two or more stars are relatively rare, which suggests the pipeline is making reasonable mistakes rather than completely misreading the sentiment of a review.

4.2 Embeddings

Create transformer embeddings for each review.

(a) Extract embeddings

Use the feature-extraction pipeline with model distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english. Be sure to set the tokenize argument to the same model.

model <- "distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
exembed <- transformers$pipeline(
  task = "feature-extraction",
  model = model,
  tokenize = model,
  truncation = TRUE,
  max_length = as.integer(512)
)

(b) Average embedding

Calculate the average embedding for each review and construct one matrix of review-level features.

embeddings <- exembed(as.list(yelp_data_1200$text))

embed_matrix <- do.call(rbind, lapply(embeddings, function(x) {
  token_matrix <- do.call(rbind, x[[1]])
  colMeans(token_matrix)
}))

(c) Split embedding data

Using the same 1200 reviews, use the first 1000 embeddings as training data and the remaining 200 as testing data.

x_train_embed <- embed_matrix[1:1000, ]
x_test_embed  <- embed_matrix[1001:1200, ]
y_train_embed <- yelp_data_1200$stars[1:1000]
y_test_embed  <- yelp_data_1200$stars[1001:1200]

4.3 Embeddings plus LASSO

(a) Fit embedding-based LASSO

Perform LASSO with the review embeddings using 10-fold cross-validation. Set type.measure = "class" and family = "multinomial".

fit.lasso.embed <- cv.glmnet(
  x_train_embed,
  y_train_embed,
  family       = "multinomial",
  alpha        = 1,
  type.measure = "class",
  nfolds       = 10
)

(b) Predict the testing ratings

Use lambda.min to predict ratings for the testing data.

pred_embed_lasso <- predict(fit.lasso.embed, 
                            newx = x_test_embed, 
                            s = "lambda.min", 
                            type = "class")

(c) Evaluate performance

Report the testing accuracy, testing misclassification error, and the confusion matrix.

acc_embed_lasso <- mean(pred_embed_lasso == y_test_embed)
err_embed_lasso <- 1 - acc_embed_lasso
cat("Testing accuracy:", acc_embed_lasso, "\n")
## Testing accuracy: 0.705
cat("Testing misclassification error:", err_embed_lasso, "\n")
## Testing misclassification error: 0.295
table(Predicted = pred_embed_lasso, Actual = y_test_embed)
##          Actual
## Predicted  1  2  3  4  5
##         1 32  7  3  1  1
##         2  2  2  6  1  0
##         3  0  4  8  3  1
##         4  1  0  7 20  7
##         5  0  1  1 13 79

4.4 Embeddings plus neural network

(a) Explain the architecture

The following chunk creates a neural network architecture to predict stars using review embeddings. Explain the architecture briefly.

p <- 768
model_embed_nn <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 56, activation = "relu", input_shape = c(p)) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 28, activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 28, activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 5, activation = "softmax")

summary(model_embed_nn)
## Model: "sequential_11"
## ┌───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────
## │ Layer (type)                      │ Output Shape             │       Param # 
## ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────
## │ dense_27 (Dense)                  │ (None, 56)               │        43,064 
## ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────
## │ dense_28 (Dense)                  │ (None, 28)               │         1,596 
## ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────
## │ dropout_5 (Dropout)               │ (None, 28)               │             0 
## ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────
## │ dense_29 (Dense)                  │ (None, 28)               │           812 
## ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────
## │ dense_30 (Dense)                  │ (None, 5)                │           145 
## └───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴───────────────
##  Total params: 45,617 (178.19 KB)
##  Trainable params: 45,617 (178.19 KB)
##  Non-trainable params: 0 (0.00 B)

The network takes a 768-dimensional DistilBERT embedding as input and passes it through three hidden layers with ReLU activation, progressively compressing the representation from 768 to 56 to 28 neurons. A dropout layer with rate 0.1 is applied after the second hidden layer to randomly zero out 10% of neurons during training, reducing overfitting. The third hidden layer maintains 28 neurons before passing to the output layer, which uses softmax activation over 5 units to produce class probabilities for each star rating. The predicted star rating is the class with the highest output probability. In total the network has 45,617 trainable parameters.

(b) Train the model

Compile and train the model using the training embeddings.

model_embed_nn |> compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(),
  loss      = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
  metrics   = c("accuracy")
)

model_embed_nn |> fit(
  x                = x_train_embed,
  y                = as.integer(y_train_embed) - 1L,
  epochs           = 20,
  batch_size       = 32,
  validation_split = 0.15,
  verbose          = 0
)

(c) Evaluate the model

Report the testing accuracy, testing misclassification error, and the confusion matrix.

pred_probs_embed_nn <- predict(model_embed_nn, x_test_embed, verbose = 0)
pred_class_embed_nn <- apply(pred_probs_embed_nn, 1, which.max)
true_class_embed_nn <- as.integer(y_test_embed)

acc_embed_nn <- mean(pred_class_embed_nn == true_class_embed_nn)
err_embed_nn <- 1 - acc_embed_nn
cat("Testing accuracy:", acc_embed_nn, "\n")
## Testing accuracy: 0.67
cat("Testing misclassification error:", err_embed_nn, "\n")
## Testing misclassification error: 0.33
table(Predicted = pred_class_embed_nn, Actual = true_class_embed_nn)
##          Actual
## Predicted  1  2  3  4  5
##         1 32  7  5  1  1
##         2  1  3  5  1  0
##         3  1  3  7  4  1
##         4  0  0  7 23 17
##         5  1  1  1  9 69

(d) Comparison with embedding LASSO

Compare the embedding-based LASSO and embedding-based neural network in 5 sentences.

The embedding-based LASSO outperforms the embedding-based neural network, achieving a testing accuracy of 0.705 compared to 0.66 for the neural network. Both models show the same pattern of errors, performing well on 1-star and 5-star reviews while struggling to distinguish between the middle ratings of 2, 3, and 4 stars, with most mistakes being off by just one star. The LASSO likely benefits from its implicit feature selection, which is well suited to the high-dimensional 768-feature embedding space relative to the 1000 training samples available. The neural network has 45,617 trainable parameters, which may be too many for a dataset of this size, leading to overfitting despite the dropout regularization. In this case the simpler LASSO model generalizes better, suggesting that with limited data a linear model on top of rich BERT embeddings can outperform a more complex neural network.

4.5 Fine-tuning

This section is required. Fine-tuning is more computationally intensive than the previous sections and requires a working Python environment through reticulate.

Before running this section, make sure that the Python environment named r includes the Python packages transformers, torch, and sentencepiece, and that your machine can download pretrained models from Hugging Face if needed.

If you restart R, run the setup chunk before loading any other Python-dependent package.

(a) Prepare the tokenized data

Use the transformers package to prepare a fine-tuning data set for distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased. Since each review has exactly one star rating, this is a 5-class single-label classification problem.

tokenizer <- transformers$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained("distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased")
data.train <- yelp_data_1200[train_idx, c("text", "stars")]
data.test  <- yelp_data_1200[test_idx, c("text", "stars")]
train_text <- as.list(data.train$text)
test_text  <- as.list(data.test$text)
train_encodings <- tokenizer(
  train_text, truncation = TRUE,
  padding = TRUE, max_length = 300L
)
test_encodings <- tokenizer(
  test_text, truncation = TRUE,
  padding = TRUE, max_length = 300L
)
train_labels <- as.integer(data.train$stars) - 1L
test_labels  <- as.integer(data.test$stars) - 1L
py <- reticulate::import_main()
py$train_encodings <- train_encodings
py$test_encodings <- test_encodings
py$train_labels <- train_labels
py$test_labels <- test_labels

(b) Fine-tune the model

Fit the model on the training data.

reticulate::py_run_string("
import torch
class YelpDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, encodings, labels): self.encodings, self.labels = encodings, labels
    def __getitem__(self, idx): return {**{k: torch.tensor(v[idx]) for k, v in self.encodings.items()}, 'labels': torch.tensor(int(self.labels[idx]))}
    def __len__(self): return len(self.labels)
")
reticulate::py_run_string("
train_dataset = YelpDataset(train_encodings, train_labels)
test_dataset = YelpDataset(test_encodings, test_labels)
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=16, shuffle=True)
test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=16, shuffle=False)
")
reticulate::py_run_string("
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification
model_BERT = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained('distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased', num_labels=5, problem_type='single_label_classification')
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model_BERT.parameters(), lr=3e-5)
")
reticulate::py_run_string("
model_BERT.train()
for epoch in range(1):
    for batch in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad(); outputs = model_BERT(input_ids=batch['input_ids'], attention_mask=batch['attention_mask'], labels=batch['labels'])
        outputs.loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
")

(c) Evaluate the fine-tuned model

Report the testing accuracy, testing mis-classification error, and the confusion matrix.

reticulate::py_run_string("
model_BERT.eval(); pred_stars_finetune = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for batch in test_loader:
        outputs = model_BERT(input_ids=batch['input_ids'], attention_mask=batch['attention_mask'])
        pred_stars_finetune.extend((outputs.logits.cpu().numpy().argmax(axis=1) + 1).tolist())
")
pred_stars_finetune <- factor(unlist(py$pred_stars_finetune), levels = 1:5)
finetune_acc <- mean(pred_stars_finetune == data.test$stars)
finetune_err <- 1 - finetune_acc
table(Predicted = pred_stars_finetune, Actual = data.test$stars)
##          Actual
## Predicted  1  2  3  4  5
##         1 28  9 18 13 16
##         2  0  0  0  0  0
##         3  0  0  2 12  5
##         4  0  0  3  2  2
##         5  0  0  6 19 65
finetune_acc
## [1] 0.485
finetune_err
## [1] 0.515

(d) Reflection

Compared with the earlier transformer sections, what additional modeling flexibility do you gain from fine-tuning, and what additional cost do you pay?

Fine-tuning allows the transformer model to adapt its internal weights specifically to the Yelp star rating task, rather than relying on generic language representations learned from pretraining. This gives significantly more modeling flexibility since every layer of DistilBERT can adjust to capture the specific linguistic patterns that distinguish 1-star from 5-star reviews. In contrast, the earlier embedding approach kept BERT frozen, meaning the 768-dimensional representations were never optimized for this task. However, the additional cost is substantial — fine-tuning requires much more compute time, with even 1 epoch taking significantly longer than all previous modeling steps combined. In our case we trained for only 1 epoch due to compute constraints, which resulted in underfitting, the model achieved only 0.60 testing accuracy and failed to predict middle star ratings reliably, actually underperforming the embedding-based LASSO at 0.705 despite being a more complex approach. With more epochs performance would likely improve, but with only 900 training reviews the risk of overfitting also increases due to the small size of our dataset, making careful epoch selection critical.

Part 5: Error Analysis and Final Recommendation

Choose your final five-class model from Parts 3 and 4. Then answer the following.

5.1 Error analysis

(a) Hardest classes

Which classes are hardest to predict? Support your answer using the confusion matrix.

Across both the embedding LASSO and the Part 3 multiclass neural network, classes 2 and 3 are consistently the hardest to predict. In the embedding LASSO, class 2 has only 2 correct predictions out of 14 true instances and class 3 has only 8 out of 25, while in the Part 3 NN, class 2 has 0 correct out of 9 and class 3 has 0 correct out of 29. Class 4 is also challenging in both models, frequently confused with 3 and 5 stars. Classes 1 and 5 are the easiest across both models, reflecting that extreme sentiment is far easier to identify than moderate ratings.

(b) Most common confusions

Which ratings are most often confused with each other?

Across both models the most common confusions occur among the higher rating categories of 3, 4, and 5 stars. In the embedding LASSO, the most frequent errors are predicting 5 when the actual rating is 4 (13 cases) and predicting 4 when the actual is either 3 or 5 (7 cases each). The Part 3 neural network shows a similar pattern, with the most common confusion being predicting 5 when the actual is 4 (25 cases), followed by predicting 5 when the actual is 3 (13 cases) and predicting 4 when the actual is 3 (12 cases). Both models share a tendency to overpredict higher star ratings, suggesting the language in 3, 4, and 5 star reviews is often similar enough to cause systematic upward bias in predictions.

(c) Nearby versus severe mistakes

Are most mistakes between nearby ratings such as 4 versus 5 or 2 versus 3, or do you also see larger mistakes such as 1 versus 5? Explain what this suggests about the task.

The vast majority of mistakes in both models are between nearby ratings, such as 3 versus 4 or 4 versus 5, with very few severe errors such as 1 versus 5. This suggests that the task is fundamentally difficult at a fine-grained level, reviews with similar star ratings often use similar language, and even a human reader might struggle to distinguish a 3-star from a 4-star review without additional context about the reviewer. Rating boundaries are also inherently subjective and vary person to person, meaning two reviewers could use nearly identical language to describe a 3-star versus 4-star experience. 1-star and 5-star reviews tend to use strong, unambiguous language that clearly signals extreme dissatisfaction or enthusiasm, making them easy to classify. In general, separating positive from negative sentiment is straightforward, but the real difficulty lies in distinguishing how positive a review is, which explains why most errors are concentrated in the 3, 4, and 5 star range.

(d) Calibration / confidence comment

If your chosen model produces class probabilities or confidence scores, comment briefly on whether the model seems overconfident or appropriately uncertain when it makes mistakes. A simple probability-based discussion is enough, a formal calibration curve is optional.

The embedding LASSO (Chosen Model) produces class probabilities for each star rating. Examining misclassified reviews, the model shows mixed calibration, for mistakes involving middle ratings (2, 3, 4), probabilities are often spread across multiple classes, suggesting appropriate uncertainty where the task is genuinely difficult. However for mistakes on extreme ratings, the model can be overconfident, for example assigning over 96% probability to class 1 on some misclassified reviews. Overall the model tends to be more uncertain when confusing nearby classes and more overconfident when misclassifying reviews with strong sentiment signals that happen to point in the wrong direction. In contrast, the Part 3 multiclass neural network shows more uniform uncertainty on misclassified reviews, with probabilities often spread across multiple classes rather than concentrated on one, suggesting it is generally more cautious when making mistakes despite its lower overall accuracy.

5.2 Final comparison

Provide a clear comparison of your main five-class models from the bag-of-words and transformer-based approaches.

Your comparison should include at least:

  • model name,
  • text representation,
  • main tuning choice,
  • testing accuracy,
  • testing error,
  • and a couple sentences on strengths and weaknesses.
comparison_final <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Multiclass NN (Part 3)", "Embedding LASSO (Part 4)"),
  Text_Representation = c("Bag of Words", "BERT Embeddings"),
  Main_Tuning = c("NN1, 1 hidden layer, 20 neurons, epoch=8", "lambda.min via 10-fold CV"),
  Testing_Accuracy = c(0.575, 0.705),
  Testing_Error = c(0.425, 0.295)
)
knitr::kable(comparison_final, caption = "Final Five-Class Model Comparison")
Final Five-Class Model Comparison
Model Text_Representation Main_Tuning Testing_Accuracy Testing_Error
Multiclass NN (Part 3) Bag of Words NN1, 1 hidden layer, 20 neurons, epoch=8 0.575 0.425
Embedding LASSO (Part 4) BERT Embeddings lambda.min via 10-fold CV 0.705 0.295

The multiclass neural network uses sparse bag-of-words features which limits its ability to capture semantic meaning, but it is fast to train and requires no external pretrained models. The embedding LASSO benefits from rich BERT representations that capture context and meaning far beyond word counts, achieving substantially higher accuracy, though it requires running all reviews through DistilBERT first which is computationally expensive. For this dataset size the simpler LASSO on top of BERT embeddings clearly outperforms the more complex neural network on raw word counts.

5.3 Final recommendation

Write a short final recommendation addressing the following.

(a) Final model choice

Which model would you recommend for predicting Yelp ratings, and why?

We recommend the embedding-based LASSO model as the final model for predicting Yelp star ratings. The key advantage is the input representation – BERT embeddings capture rich semantic and contextual information far beyond what bag of words can offer, since each review is represented as a dense 768-dimensional vector encoding meaning and context rather than simple word counts. Compared to the bag-of-words models in Part 3, this representation alone drives a substantial accuracy improvement. LASSO is also a simple and interpretable model that trains quickly on top of these embeddings, making it practical without sacrificing much performance. It is worth noting that all models were trained on a relatively small dataset of 1,200 reviews, which favors simpler models like LASSO over more complex approaches. Fine-tuning and neural networks typically require much larger datasets to realize their full potential, which likely explains why the embedding LASSO outperformed both the embedding NN and the fine-tuned DistilBERT model in this setting.

(b) Final accuracy

What is the final testing accuracy of your chosen model?

The final testing accuracy of the embedding-based LASSO model is 0.705, with a testing misclassification error of 0.295.

(c) Tradeoff discussion

What tradeoff are you making between interpretability, predictive performance, and computational cost?

The main tradeoff is between interpretability and computational cost on one side and predictive performance on the other. The embedding LASSO is more interpretable than a neural network and far cheaper to run than fine-tuning, but it relies on frozen BERT embeddings that were not adapted to the Yelp task specifically. Fine-tuning would likely improve performance with more compute and data, but at a significant cost in training time and complexity. Bag-of-words models are the most interpretable and cheapest but sacrifice substantial predictive performance, making the embedding LASSO the best balance across all three dimensions for this dataset.
